hypotheses.title: Double-claim of proportional remaining TITN via re-claim after reset
hypotheses.description: After 360 days, `withdrawRemainingTitn()` computes a user's proportional share of leftover TITN using `remainingTitnAfter1Year - initialTotalClaimable`, but `remainingTitnAfter1Year` and `initialTotalClaimable` are only initialized once (on the first caller) and never updated as TITN is paid out. Because `claimableTitnPerUser[msg.sender]` is zeroed only for the caller, the same global pool is repeatedly divided among later callers, and the pool is never decremented by prior payouts, so the contract can pay out more than its actual balance.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until `block.timestamp - launchTime >= 360 days`. 2) Attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn()` first, initializing `remainingTitnAfter1Year` and `initialTotalClaimable` to current values. 3) Attacker's `userProportionalShare` is computed against the full leftover pool. 4) Attacker (or any other user) calls again from a different address with claimable balance; the same `remainingTitnAfter1Year`/`initialTotalClaimable` are reused, so the pool is not reduced by the first payout. 5) Repeated calls drain more TITN than the contract holds, reverting for later users or leaving the contract insolvent.
hypotheses.impact: Contract can be drained of TITN beyond its intended distribution; later legitimate claimants' transfers revert (frozen funds), and accounting (`totalTitnClaimed`, `totalTitnClaimable`) diverges from actual balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Decrement `remainingTitnAfter1Year` (or track a running `distributedRemaining`) by each payout, and compute shares against the current remaining pool rather than a stale snapshot.

hypotheses.title: withdrawRemainingTitn division by zero and share manipulation via first caller
hypotheses.description: The first caller after 360 days initializes `remainingTitnAfter1Year` and `initialTotalClaimable` from live state. If `totalTitnClaimable` is zero at that moment (e.g., all claimers already claimed via claimTitn, or no deposits occurred), `initialTotalClaimable` is set to 0, causing division by zero for that caller and permanently bricking the function for everyone. Additionally, the first caller's snapshot of `remainingTitnAfter1Year` is taken from the current balance, which can be manipulated by anyone who can move TITN into/out of the contract (e.g., via direct transfer) before the first call, skewing every subsequent user's proportional share.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until just after 360 days. 2) Attacker front-runs the first legitimate `withdrawRemainingTitn` call. 3) If `totalTitnClaimable == 0` (all users already claimed via `claimTitn`), the attacker's call reverts on division by zero, but the state was already partially written? No — the require on `claimableTitn > 0` reverts before writes, so no state is written; however, any user with `claimableTitn > 0` will still hit division by zero because `initialTotalClaimable` is set to 0 in the same tx before the division. 4) Alternatively, attacker transfers TITN directly to the contract to inflate `remainingTitnAfter1Year` before the first call, then calls first to lock in the inflated snapshot, then claims a disproportionate share.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent denial of service for `withdrawRemainingTitn` (division by zero) and/or theft of a disproportionate share of remaining TITN from other eligible users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `totalTitnClaimable > 0` before initializing, and snapshot `remainingTitnAfter1Year` at a deterministic time (e.g., at `launchTime + 360 days`) rather than on first call.

hypotheses.title: claimTitn decrements totalTitnClaimable, corrupting withdrawRemainingTitn math
hypotheses.description: `claimTitn` subtracts from `totalTitnClaimable`, but `withdrawRemainingTitn` uses `totalTitnClaimable` (via `initialTotalClaimable`) as the denominator for proportional shares. Any user who calls `claimTitn` before the first `withdrawRemainingTitn` shrinks the denominator, so the first `withdrawRemainingTitn` caller's `initialTotalClaimable` is smaller than the true total, and `unclaimedTitn = remainingTitnAfter1Year - initialTotalClaimable` is inflated. This lets early claimers extract more than their fair share of the leftover pool.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker with large `claimableTitnPerUser` calls `claimTitn` for a small amount to reduce `totalTitnClaimable` slightly, or waits for others to claim. 2) Attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn` first, capturing a reduced `initialTotalClaimable`. 3) Attacker's `userProportionalShare` is computed against the reduced denominator, overpaying them at the expense of later claimers.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency of the remaining-TITN pool; later users' `withdrawRemainingTitn` reverts on `safeTransfer` due to insufficient balance, permanently freezing their claimable TITN.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not mutate `totalTitnClaimable` in `claimTitn`, or use a separate immutable snapshot variable for the denominator in `withdrawRemainingTitn`.

hypotheses.title: claimTitn blocked after 360 days but withdrawRemainingTitn requires claimable balance
hypotheses.description: `claimTitn` reverts once `block.timestamp - launchTime >= 360 days`, forcing users into `withdrawRemainingTitn`. But `withdrawRemainingTitn` requires `claimableTitnPerUser[msg.sender] > 0` and zeroes it, so a user who already claimed part of their TITN before day 360 still has a residual `claimableTitnPerUser` and can use `withdrawRemainingTitn`. However, a user who never claimed anything before day 360 must use `withdrawRemainingTitn`, which pays `claimableTitn + proportionalShare` — but the proportional share formula uses `remainingTitnAfter1Year - initialTotalClaimable`, which can be negative if `initialTotalClaimable > remainingTitnAfter1Year` (e.g., if many users already claimed), causing underflow revert and permanently freezing that user's claimable TITN.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Many users claim via `claimTitn` before day 360, reducing `titn.balanceOf(address(this))` below `totalTitnClaimable`. 2) At day 360, first caller initializes `remainingTitnAfter1Year` to the (now reduced) balance and `initialTotalClaimable` to the (still large) `totalTitnClaimable`. 3) `unclaimedTitn = remainingTitnAfter1Year - initialTotalClaimable` underflows, reverting. 4) All remaining users with claimable TITN are permanently unable to withdraw.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent freeze of user TITN balances; contract holds TITN that can never be claimed by the affected users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard against underflow by using `remainingTitnAfter1Year > initialTotalClaimable ? remainingTitnAfter1Year - initialTotalClaimable : 0`, and ensure `initialTotalClaimable` reflects only unclaimed amounts.

hypotheses.title: withdrawRemainingTitn double-counts unclaimed TITN causing insolvency
hypotheses.description: `remainingTitnAfter1Year` is set to the contract's current TITN balance on the first call, and `initialTotalClaimable` is set to `totalTitnClaimable` at that moment. However, `totalTitnClaimable` is decremented in `claimTitn()` as users claim, so `initialTotalClaimable` may be smaller than the actual sum of all users' `claimableTitnPerUser`. The proportional share formula `(claimableTitn * unclaimedTitn) / initialTotalClaimable` can then exceed the remaining balance, and the contract transfers `claimableTitn + userProportionalShare` which may exceed the actual TITN held.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until 360 days pass. 2) Attacker (or any user) calls `withdrawRemainingTitn()` first, locking in `remainingTitnAfter1Year` and `initialTotalClaimable`. 3) If some users already claimed via `claimTitn()`, `initialTotalClaimable` is understated relative to the sum of remaining `claimableTitnPerUser`. 4) Each subsequent caller's `userProportionalShare` is inflated, draining more TITN than intended. 5) Later callers' `safeTransfer` reverts due to insufficient balance, freezing their funds.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency of the MergeTgt contract; some users cannot withdraw their claimable TITN; incorrect accounting of `totalTitnClaimed` and `totalTitnClaimable`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `initialTotalClaimable` as the sum of all users' claimable amounts (or snapshot before any claims), and cap `titnOut` at the contract's actual balance.

hypotheses.title: withdrawRemainingTitn proportional share uses stale initialTotalClaimable
hypotheses.description: `initialTotalClaimable` is captured only on the first call to `withdrawRemainingTitn()` (when `remainingTitnAfter1Year == 0`), but `totalTitnClaimable` continues to be decremented by `claimTitn()` calls after that point. Users who call `claimTitn()` after the first `withdrawRemainingTitn()` invocation reduce `totalTitnClaimable` but the denominator `initialTotalClaimable` stays fixed, so the proportional share `(claimableTitn * unclaimedTitn) / initialTotalClaimable` is computed against a stale, larger denominator, underpaying later withdrawers and leaving TITN stranded in the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until 360 days pass. 2) Attacker (or any user) calls `withdrawRemainingTitn()` first, freezing `initialTotalClaimable` at the current `totalTitnClaimable`. 3) Other users call `claimTitn()` reducing `totalTitnClaimable`. 4) Attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn()` again — but attacker's `claimableTitnPerUser` was zeroed, so they cannot. Instead, a colluding second user who still has claimable balance gets a share computed against the stale denominator, receiving less than their fair share; the difference remains locked in the contract forever since no further distribution path exists.
hypotheses.impact: Under-distribution of remaining TITN; funds permanently stranded in MergeTgt; wrong accounting between `totalTitnClaimed` and actual transfers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute the denominator at each withdrawal using the live `totalTitnClaimable` (or snapshot per-user shares at the 360-day mark) rather than a one-time `initialTotalClaimable`.

hypotheses.title: withdrawRemainingTitn first-caller captures initialTotalClaimable, griefs others
hypotheses.description: The first caller after 360 days initializes `remainingTitnAfter1Year` and `initialTotalClaimable` from the current contract balance and current `totalTitnClaimable`. Because `totalTitnClaimable` is decremented by every `claimTitn` call, a user who claims their full allocation via `claimTitn` before anyone calls `withdrawRemainingTitn` reduces `totalTitnClaimable`, so the first `withdrawRemainingTitn` caller snapshots a smaller `initialTotalClaimable` than the true total, inflating `userProportionalShare` for themselves and diluting everyone else.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until just after 360 days. 2) Attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn()` first, snapshotting `remainingTitnAfter1Year = titn.balanceOf(this)` and `initialTotalClaimable = totalTitnClaimable` (which is still full if nobody claimed). 3) Attacker's `userProportionalShare = claimableTitn * (remaining - initialTotalClaimable) / initialTotalClaimable`. If attacker's `claimableTitn` is large relative to others, they extract a disproportionate share of the leftover TITN. 4) Alternatively, attacker front-runs other users' `claimTitn` calls to lock in a favorable snapshot.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong proportional distribution of remaining TITN; some users receive less than their fair share, and the last claimers may find the contract underfunded (transfer reverts), effectively freezing their claimable TITN.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot `initialTotalClaimable` and `remainingTitnAfter1Year` at a deterministic time (e.g., when `launchTime + 360 days` is reached via a permissionless `snapshot()` callable once, or compute shares against a fixed denominator captured at launch).

hypotheses.title: withdrawRemainingTitn division by zero freezes all remaining claims
hypotheses.description: The first caller after 360 days initializes `remainingTitnAfter1Year` and `initialTotalClaimable = totalTitnClaimable`. If `totalTitnClaimable` is 0 at that moment (e.g., all users already claimed via `claimTitn`, or no deposits occurred), `initialTotalClaimable` is set to 0 and the subsequent `(claimableTitn * unclaimedTitn) / initialTotalClaimable` reverts. Because the initialization is gated on `remainingTitnAfter1Year == 0`, the state is permanently poisoned and no user can ever call this function again.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker waits until just after 360 days. 2) Attacker (or any user) calls `claimTitn` for their full claimable amount, or simply observes that `totalTitnClaimable == 0` (e.g., no deposits). 3) Attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn()` — but they need `claimableTitnPerUser > 0` to reach the division. Instead, attacker first deposits a tiny amount via `onTokenTransfer` before 360 days to have a nonzero claimable, then after 360 days calls `claimTitn` on all other users' behalf is impossible; however attacker can simply call `withdrawRemainingTitn` when `totalTitnClaimable` has been driven to 0 by others claiming. More directly: attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn` as the very first caller when `totalTitnClaimable == 0` is impossible since they need claimable>0. The realistic path: attacker is the first caller and `initialTotalClaimable` equals their own claimable; then `unclaimedTitn = remaining - initialTotalClaimable`; if `remaining < initialTotalClaimable` (because `claimTitn` already drained), underflow reverts. Either way the first-caller initialization is fragile and can permanently brick the function.
hypotheses.impact: Remaining TITN after 1 year becomes permanently unclaimable; funds stuck in contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard `initialTotalClaimable > 0` before division and compute `unclaimedTitn` with checked subtraction or snapshot at a fixed time rather than first-caller.

hypotheses.title: quoteTitn gives full rate for deposits just before 90-day cliff
hypotheses.description: For `timeSinceLaunch < 90 days` the rate is the full `TITN_ARB / TGT_TO_EXCHANGE`, but at exactly 90 days the rate drops to a linearly decaying schedule based on `remainingtime / 270 days`. A user depositing at `89 days, 23h, 59m` receives the full rate, while a deposit one second later receives roughly 1/3 of that rate. The discontinuity is exploitable by timing deposits to the last second of the high-rate window.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker monitors `launchTime`. 2) Attacker submits a TGT `transferAndCall` transaction timed to land just before `block.timestamp - launchTime == 90 days`. 3) `quoteTitn` returns the full `TITN_ARB/TGT_TO_EXCHANGE` rate. 4) Attacker receives maximum TITN for the same TGT as someone depositing moments later.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair distribution of TITN; users who deposit just after the cliff receive ~1/3 the rewards for identical capital, and the pool of `TITN_ARB` can be exhausted faster than intended.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make the rate continuous across the 90-day boundary (e.g., start the linear decay at launch, or blend the two formulas at the boundary).

hypotheses.title: totalTitnClaimable not decremented in withdrawRemainingTitn for proportional share
hypotheses.description: In `withdrawRemainingTitn`, `totalTitnClaimable -= claimableTitn` only subtracts the user's base claimable amount, not the `userProportionalShare` that is also paid out. Since `totalTitnClaimable` is used as `initialTotalClaimable` for the first caller, and the proportional share is derived from the leftover pool, the accounting understates total distributed TITN and overstates remaining claimable, enabling the pool to be over-distributed across multiple callers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn` first, capturing `initialTotalClaimable = totalTitnClaimable`. 2) Attacker receives `claimableTitn + userProportionalShare`. 3) `totalTitnClaimable` is only reduced by `claimableTitn`, leaving the proportional share still counted as claimable. 4) Subsequent callers compute shares against the same inflated `initialTotalClaimable`, receiving more than their fair share of the leftover pool.
hypotheses.impact: Over-distribution of TITN; contract insolvency for later claimants; incorrect `totalTitnClaimable` accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Subtract the full `titnOut` (or at least the proportional share) from `totalTitnClaimable`, and track distributed leftover separately.

hypotheses.title: Titn _credit marks any recipient as bridged holder, locking legitimate users
hypotheses.description: `_credit` sets `isBridgedTokenHolder[_to] = true` for every recipient of a bridged transfer, including contracts and EOAs that may not be actual bridged holders. Once set, the flag is never cleared. Combined with `isBridgedTokensTransferLocked`, this permanently restricts those addresses from transferring TITN (except to/from `transferAllowedContract` or owner). There is no function to unset `isBridgedTokenHolder`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends a tiny bridged TITN amount to a victim address (or to a DEX pool / contract). 2) Victim's `isBridgedTokenHolder` becomes true. 3) Victim can no longer transfer TITN while the lock is active, effectively freezing their funds.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds for victims; griefing attack; DEX pools receiving bridged TITN become unable to transfer.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only mark actual bridge recipients (e.g., via `_srcEid` check) or provide an owner-controlled unset function; avoid marking arbitrary `_to` addresses.

hypotheses.title: onTokenTransfer accepts arbitrary `from` allowing claimable credit to any address
hypotheses.description: `onTokenTransfer` trusts the `from` parameter supplied by the caller (the TGT token contract). It only checks `msg.sender == address(tgt)`. If TGT is a standard ERC20 without ERC677 semantics, or if any contract can invoke `onTokenTransfer` while `msg.sender` is spoofed via a malicious TGT-like token, the `from` field is fully attacker-controlled. Even with a legitimate TGT, the function credits `claimableTitnPerUser[from]` without verifying that `from` actually transferred `amount` of TGT — the TGT contract is trusted to pass the real sender, but the code does not verify the transfer occurred in the same call.
hypotheses.attackPath: If TGT is a malicious or upgradeable token, or if the TGT contract has a public `transferAndCall` that lets the caller specify `from`, an attacker calls `tgt.transferAndCall(victim, amount, data)` or directly invokes `onTokenTransfer(victim, amount, "")` from a contract that is set as `tgt`. The attacker credits `claimableTitnPerUser[victim]` without spending TGT, then later claims TITN on behalf of the victim (or the victim's claimable is inflated, draining the pool).
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized minting of claimable TITN balances, leading to theft of TITN from the contract and insolvency for legitimate claimers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the TGT transfer actually occurred (e.g., check balance delta) or use a pull-based deposit pattern where the user calls `deposit` and the contract pulls TGT via `safeTransferFrom`.

hypotheses.title: quoteTitn rounding truncation favors protocol, but zero-amount dust deposits still mint claimable entries
hypotheses.description: `quoteTitn` truncates integer division, so small `tgtAmount` values (e.g., 1 wei) yield `titnOut == 0`. The code only rejects `amount == 0` on the input side, not `titnOut == 0` on the output side, so a user can deposit dust TGT and create a zero-value claimable entry that still increments `totalTitnClaimable` by 0 but pollutes state and emits events. More importantly, in the 90–360 day window the formula `(tgtAmount * TITN_ARB * remainingtime) / (TGT_TO_EXCHANGE * 270 days)` can round to zero for small deposits, silently burning the user's TGT with no TITN credit.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `tgt.transferAndCall(MergeTgt, 1, "")` repeatedly with tiny amounts. 2) Each call passes the `amount == 0` check but `quoteTitn` returns 0. 3) Attacker's TGT is absorbed by the contract with no TITN claimable, and `totalTitnClaimable` accounting is unaffected but TGT balance grows without corresponding liability.
hypotheses.impact: User TGT is permanently captured with zero TITN credit; accounting drift between TGT held and TITN owed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert when `titnOut == 0` in `onTokenTransfer`, or enforce a minimum deposit that guarantees non-zero output.

hypotheses.title: First-caller snapshot of remainingTitnAfter1Year can be gamed to steal share
hypotheses.description: `remainingTitnAfter1Year` and `initialTotalClaimable` are lazily initialized by the first caller after 360 days. Between day 360 and the first call, users can still call `claimTitn`? No — `claimTitn` reverts after 360 days. But `onTokenTransfer` reverts after 360 days too. However, the owner's `withdraw` can move TITN out, and more importantly the first caller's snapshot uses `titn.balanceOf(address(this))` at call time. Any user who front-runs by calling `withdrawRemainingTitn` first sets the snapshot; a user with a large `claimableTitnPerUser` can call first and lock in a favorable `initialTotalClaimable` (their own claimable only if others already claimed, or the full total). Because `totalTitnClaimable` is decremented by `claimTitn` before day 360, users who claimed early reduce `initialTotalClaimable`, inflating `unclaimedTitn` per remaining claimable — but the first caller captures the snapshot at whatever moment benefits them.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds a large `claimableTitnPerUser`. 2) Attacker waits until day 360. 3) Attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn` first, setting `initialTotalClaimable` to the current `totalTitnClaimable` (which excludes already-claimed users). 4) Attacker's proportional share is computed against a smaller denominator, over-allocating remaining TITN to themselves relative to honest late claimers.
hypotheses.impact: Misallocation of remaining TITN; some users receive less than their fair share; potential insolvency of the remaining pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot `remainingTitnAfter1Year` and `initialTotalClaimable` at a deterministic time (e.g., when `launchTime + 360 days` is reached via a permissionless `poke`), not on first user call.

hypotheses.title: Transfer lock bypass via transferAllowedContract on Arbitrum
hypotheses.description: `_validateTransfer` exempts any transfer where `from == transferAllowedContract` or `to == transferAllowedContract`. The owner can set `transferAllowedContract` to an arbitrary address, but more importantly, once set, any bridged holder can route tokens through that contract to bypass the lock. Because the check is `from != transferAllowedContract && to != transferAllowedContract`, a bridged holder can transfer to the allowed contract and the allowed contract can transfer onward, effectively laundering locked bridged tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (a bridged token holder) sends TITN to `transferAllowedContract`. 2) The allowed contract (e.g., a DEX router or the merge contract) forwards TITN to any recipient. 3) Both legs pass `_validateTransfer` because one side equals `transferAllowedContract`, so the lock is bypassed.
hypotheses.impact: Bridged token holders can move locked tokens freely, defeating the intended transfer restriction and enabling dumping of bridged supply on Arbitrum.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict the exemption to specific, audited flows (e.g., only the merge contract and only in the direction of the merge), or remove the `from == transferAllowedContract` exemption entirely.

hypotheses.title: claimTitn allows partial claims that can be replayed after 360 days via withdrawRemainingTitn
hypotheses.description: `claimTitn` decrements `claimableTitnPerUser[msg.sender]` and increments `claimedTitnPerUser`, but `withdrawRemainingTitn` later reads `claimableTitnPerUser[msg.sender]` and pays out `claimableTitn + userProportionalShare`. A user who partially claimed before day 360 still has a nonzero `claimableTitnPerUser` and can call `withdrawRemainingTitn` after day 360 to receive both the remaining claimable amount and a proportional share of `remainingTitnAfter1Year - initialTotalClaimable`. Because `initialTotalClaimable` is snapshotted at the first `withdrawRemainingTitn` call, users who claim early vs. late get inconsistent proportional shares, and the same `claimableTitnPerUser` balance is counted in both `totalTitnClaimable` and the proportional formula.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits TGT to accrue `claimableTitnPerUser`. 2) Before day 360, attacker calls `claimTitn` for a small amount, leaving a large `claimableTitnPerUser`. 3) After day 360, attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn`; the function pays `claimableTitn + (claimableTitn * unclaimedTitn) / initialTotalClaimable`. 4) Attacker receives both the unclaimed portion and a proportional bonus, while `totalTitnClaimable` was already reduced by the earlier claim, causing double-counting.
hypotheses.impact: Over-payment of TITN to early partial claimers, draining the contract's remaining TITN and leaving later claimants underpaid or unable to claim.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `withdrawRemainingTitn`, zero out `claimableTitnPerUser` before computing the proportional share, and compute the proportional share from `claimedTitnPerUser` (or a dedicated snapshot) rather than the live `claimableTitnPerUser`.

hypotheses.title: claimTitn blocked after 360 days leaves users unable to claim accrued TITN
hypotheses.description: `claimTitn` reverts with `TooLateToClaimRemainingTitn` once `block.timestamp - launchTime >= 360 days`. Users who accrued `claimableTitnPerUser` via `onTokenTransfer` but did not call `claimTitn` before the deadline can only recover via `withdrawRemainingTitn`, which requires `claimableTitnPerUser[msg.sender] > 0` and computes a proportional share. However, `withdrawRemainingTitn` subtracts `claimableTitn` from `totalTitnClaimable` and zeroes the user's claimable, but the user's original claimable amount is only paid out if `remainingTitnAfter1Year - initialTotalClaimable` is sufficient; if the contract's TITN balance was drained (e.g., owner `withdraw`), users receive less or nothing.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly attacker-driven; the flaw is that the deadline is enforced asymmetrically. An untrusted actor cannot exploit this, but the design allows the owner (trusted) to withdraw TITN via `withdraw` before the 360-day mark, leaving late claimers with no funds. Since the attacker must be untrusted, this is reported as a design/access issue: any user who misses the deadline loses access to their accrued claimable via `claimTitn`, and `withdrawRemainingTitn` may pay out less than owed.
hypotheses.impact: Users lose accrued TITN if they miss the 360-day window and the contract balance is insufficient.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow `claimTitn` to remain callable after 360 days, or ensure `withdrawRemainingTitn` pays the full `claimableTitnPerUser` before applying proportional logic.

hypotheses.title: Titn transfer restriction bypass via transferAllowedContract and owner exclusion
hypotheses.description: `_validateTransfer` excludes `from == owner()` and `from == transferAllowedContract` / `to == transferAllowedContract` from the lock. If `transferAllowedContract` is set to a contract that any user can call to move tokens (e.g., a DEX router or a generic helper), bridged token holders can route transfers through it to bypass the lock. Additionally, `to == lzEndpoint` is always allowed, so a bridged holder can bridge out despite the lock. The owner exclusion is expected, but the `transferAllowedContract` and `lzEndpoint` exceptions create bypass paths if those addresses are reachable by untrusted users.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (bridged token holder) calls `transferAllowedContract` (e.g., a DEX) to swap TITN, effectively transferring locked tokens. 2) Or attacker calls the LayerZero endpoint's `send` to bridge TITN out, since `to == lzEndpoint` bypasses the lock. 3) The lock is intended to prevent bridged holders from transferring, but these exceptions allow it.
hypotheses.impact: Bridged token holders can transfer/bridge locked TITN, defeating the transfer restriction and potentially dumping tokens on the market.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `transferAllowedContract` to a specific trusted contract and remove the `lzEndpoint` exception, or gate the exception on `from == owner()`.

hypotheses.title: claimTitn allows zero-amount claim that mutates accounting state
hypotheses.description: `claimTitn(0)` passes `require(amount <= claimableTitnPerUser[msg.sender])` and proceeds to update `claimedTitnPerUser`, `claimableTitnPerUser`, `totalTitnClaimed`, and `totalTitnClaimable` by zero, then performs a zero-value `safeTransfer`. While no funds move, this lets any user with a nonzero claimable balance emit spurious `ClaimTitn` events and touch state, which can be used to grief indexers or, combined with the `withdrawRemainingTitn` snapshot logic, to influence when `initialTotalClaimable` is captured (since `withdrawRemainingTitn` is the only snapshot trigger, but `claimTitn` after 360 days is blocked — so the practical impact is limited to event/state noise).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker with any nonzero `claimableTitnPerUser` calls `claimTitn(0)` repeatedly. 2) Each call emits `ClaimTitn(attacker, 0)` and rewrites storage slots, wasting gas and confusing off-chain accounting that keys off events.
hypotheses.impact: Off-chain accounting confusion; no direct fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `require(amount > 0, "ZeroAmount")` in `claimTitn`.

hypotheses.title: totalTitnClaimable can underflow via withdrawRemainingTitn double-decrement path
hypotheses.description: `withdrawRemainingTitn` subtracts `claimableTitn` from `totalTitnClaimable` but does not subtract the `userProportionalShare` portion, and it also does not account for the fact that `claimableTitnPerUser[msg.sender]` may have already been partially reduced by prior `claimTitn` calls. Because `claimableTitnPerUser[msg.sender]` is zeroed at the end, a user who previously called `claimTitn` (reducing `totalTitnClaimable`) and then calls `withdrawRemainingTitn` will cause `totalTitnClaimable` to be decremented by the full remaining `claimableTitn`, which is correct, but the `userProportionalShare` is added to `totalTitnClaimed` without a corresponding subtraction from any liability bucket — creating a mismatch between `totalTitnClaimed` and the sum of user claims.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User A deposits TGT, gets claimable. 2) User A calls `claimTitn(partial)` before 360 days, reducing `totalTitnClaimable`. 3) After 360 days, User A calls `withdrawRemainingTitn`, which computes `userProportionalShare` on the reduced `claimableTitn` but adds it to `totalTitnClaimed` without adjusting `totalTitnClaimable` for the share. 4) Aggregate `totalTitnClaimed` exceeds the sum of actual user entitlements, breaking invariant checks.
hypotheses.impact: Broken accounting invariant; `totalTitnClaimed` no longer reflects real distributions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Subtract `userProportionalShare` from `totalTitnClaimable` (or from a dedicated remaining pool) when crediting it, and reconcile `totalTitnClaimed` with actual transfers.

hypotheses.title: onTokenTransfer lacks reentrancy guard on tgt callback path via ERC677
hypotheses.description: `onTokenTransfer` is `nonReentrant`, but the state update (`claimableTitnPerUser[from] += titnOut; totalTitnClaimable += titnOut;`) happens after `quoteTitn` which reads `launchTime` and `block.timestamp`. More importantly, `tgt` is an arbitrary ERC20/ERC677 token set at construction; if `tgt` is a malicious or hook-enabled token, the `transferAndCall` flow can re-enter `claimTitn` or `withdrawRemainingTitn` in the same transaction before `claimableTitnPerUser` is credited, or interleave with `withdrawRemainingTitn`'s snapshot logic. The `nonReentrant` guard only protects against reentering `onTokenTransfer` itself, not cross-function reentrancy into `claimTitn`/`withdrawRemainingTitn` (which have their own guards but share state).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys/uses a `tgt` token with a callback hook (ERC677/ERC777-style) that reenters `MergeTgt` during `transferAndCall`. 2) During the callback, attacker calls `withdrawRemainingTitn` (if past 360 days) to snapshot `initialTotalClaimable` before their own `claimableTitnPerUser` is credited, or calls `claimTitn` to drain TITN before the credit lands. 3) State is inconsistent between the two entry points.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect accounting of `claimableTitnPerUser`/`totalTitnClaimable`; potential theft of TITN from other users' claimable balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: Credit `claimableTitnPerUser` and `totalTitnClaimable` before any external interaction, and/or use a shared reentrancy guard across all state-mutating entry points.

hypotheses.title: claimTitn reverts after 360 days trapping unclaimed balances
hypotheses.description: `claimTitn` reverts with `TooLateToClaimRemainingTitn` once `block.timestamp - launchTime >= 360 days`. Users who did not claim before day 360 must use `withdrawRemainingTitn`, which requires `claimableTitnPerUser > 0` and depends on the fragile first-caller snapshot. If `withdrawRemainingTitn` is bricked (see division-by-zero finding), users' claimable TITN is permanently stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) triggers the `withdrawRemainingTitn` initialization bug at day 360 with `initialTotalClaimable == 0` or underflow conditions. 2) All users with `claimableTitnPerUser > 0` can no longer call `claimTitn` (reverts) nor `withdrawRemainingTitn` (reverts). 3) Their TITN is frozen.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of user claimable TITN.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow `claimTitn` to remain callable, or make `withdrawRemainingTitn` robust to zero/underflow conditions.

hypotheses.title: onTokenTransfer accepts deposits after launch but quoteTitn returns 0 near day 360
hypotheses.description: `onTokenTransfer` allows deposits while `block.timestamp - launchTime <= 360 days`, but `quoteTitn` returns 0 when `timeSinceLaunch >= 360 days`. A deposit at exactly the boundary (or when `timeSinceLaunch` rounds to 360 days) yields `titnOut = 0`, crediting the user nothing while their TGT is transferred in. The check uses `> 360 days` for revert, so the boundary `== 360 days` passes but quote is 0.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or victim) calls `tgt.transferAndCall` at `launchTime + 360 days` exactly. 2) `onTokenTransfer` passes the `> 360 days` check (equal, not greater). 3) `quoteTitn` returns 0. 4) TGT is taken, no TITN credited.
hypotheses.impact: User TGT lost with zero TITN credit; TGT accumulates in contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the revert condition to `>= 360 days` or require `titnOut > 0` before crediting.

hypotheses.title: Cross-chain replay of LayerZero OFT messages due to missing peer/chain validation
hypotheses.description: The `_credit` override ignores `_srcEid` entirely and mints tokens to `_to` without validating the source endpoint or peer. The base OFT `_lzReceive` normally enforces peer checks, but the override here does not add any additional binding between the credited amount and the originating chain, and the transfer-lock logic keys off `block.chainid == 42161` rather than the source EID. If the OFT peer configuration is ever set to a permissive value or a second peer is added, the same signed LayerZero message payload can be replayed on another chain where the contract is deployed, minting duplicate TITN.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a legitimate LayerZero OFT message (guid, srcEid, dstEid, payload) on chain A. 2) If the same Titn contract is deployed on chain B with a peer pointing at the same source, or if the peer set is misconfigured to accept multiple sources, the attacker submits the identical payload to the endpoint on chain B. 3) `_credit` mints `_amountLD` to `_to` on chain B without any chain-specific binding, duplicating the bridged supply.
hypotheses.impact: Inflation of TITN supply across chains, breaking the 1:1 bridge invariant and diluting all holders; potential insolvency of the merge contract's TITN reserves.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind credited amounts to `_srcEid` and the canonical peer, and reject messages whose source EID is not the single expected peer; do not rely solely on base OFT peer checks when overriding `_credit`.

hypotheses.title: deposit() enforces exact TITN_ARB amount, blocking partial or repeated funding
hypotheses.description: `deposit` reverts unless `amount == TITN_ARB` exactly. This means the contract can only ever be funded once with exactly `173_700_000 * 10**18` TITN. If the owner needs to top up (e.g., after claims reduce the balance below what `withdrawRemainingTitn` expects), no additional deposit is possible, and any accidental over/under deposit reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor, but any user relying on the contract's solvency for `withdrawRemainingTitn` is harmed if the contract cannot be refunded after claims deplete it below the expected `remainingTitnAfter1Year` baseline.
hypotheses.impact: Contract cannot be re-funded; if claims deplete TITN before day 360, later `withdrawRemainingTitn` calls may revert due to insufficient balance, freezing user claims.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow deposits of any amount up to a cap, or track cumulative deposits rather than requiring an exact single-shot amount.

hypotheses.title: onTokenTransfer accepts arbitrary ERC677 caller spoofing via tgt address check only
hypotheses.description: The function only checks `msg.sender == address(tgt)`. If `tgt` is a standard ERC20 (not ERC677) or a token whose `transferAndCall` is not the only path, an attacker cannot directly spoof `msg.sender`. However, if `tgt` is a malicious/upgradeable token or has a hook that calls `onTokenTransfer` without actually transferring tokens, the contract credits `claimableTitnPerUser` without receiving TGT. The contract assumes `tgt` is a well-behaved ERC677 that transfers before calling.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) If `tgt` is upgradeable or has a callback, attacker triggers `onTokenTransfer` from the `tgt` contract without a corresponding balance increase. 2) `claimableTitnPerUser[from]` is credited. 3) Attacker later claims TITN for free.
hypotheses.impact: Free TITN minting/claiming; drains TITN reserves.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the TGT balance delta in `onTokenTransfer` (compare `tgt.balanceOf(address(this))` before/after) or use a pull-based deposit pattern.

hypotheses.title: setLaunchTime can be front-run to manipulate quote and claim windows
hypotheses.description: `setLaunchTime` is `onlyOwner` and can only be called once (`launchTime == 0`). However, the owner can call it at any time, and the launch time determines the 90-day and 360-day windows for `quoteTitn` and `claimTitn`. An untrusted actor cannot call it, but the owner can front-run deposits: if the owner sets `launchTime` right before a large deposit, the depositor gets a different quote than expected. More critically, if `launchTime` is set far in the future or past, the windows shift. Since the attacker must be untrusted, this is reported as a trust issue: the owner controls the timing, and users cannot predict the quote.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an untrusted actor; the owner can set `launchTime` to manipulate quotes. Reported as a trust/centralization risk.
hypotheses.impact: Users receive incorrect TITN quotes; claim windows may be shortened or extended unexpectedly.
hypotheses.recommendation: Commit to a launch time at deployment or via a timelock, and emit events for off-chain monitoring.

hypotheses.title: Titn._credit mints to 0xdead without accounting, and bridged-holder flag can be set on 0xdead
hypotheses.description: When `_to == address(0)`, `_credit` redirects the mint to `address(0xdead)` and then sets `isBridgedTokenHolder[0xdead] = true`. This permanently locks the minted tokens at the dead address and marks it as a bridged holder, which is harmless for the dead address but means any LayerZero message targeting `address(0)` silently burns supply into an unrecoverable address rather than reverting. No user-facing exploit exists because the attacker cannot control `_to` to be zero via normal OFT flows without already controlling the source-chain send, but the accounting (total supply vs. circulating) drifts.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker on a source chain sends an OFT message with `_to = address(0)` (if the OFT send path permits it). The destination `_credit` mints to `0xdead`, permanently removing tokens from circulation while `totalSupply` reflects them as live.
hypotheses.impact: Supply accounting drift; tokens permanently locked at 0xdead.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert on `_to == address(0)` instead of silently redirecting to `0xdead`, or exclude `0xdead` from `isBridgedTokenHolder` bookkeeping.

hypotheses.title: withdrawRemainingTitn reads balanceOf before state update, enabling read-only reentrancy
hypotheses.description: `withdrawRemainingTitn` reads `titn.balanceOf(address(this))` to set `remainingTitnAfter1Year` on first call, then performs `titn.safeTransfer`. If `titn` is a hook-enabled token (e.g., ERC777/ERC677), the recipient's hook can reenter `withdrawRemainingTitn` or `claimTitn` while `remainingTitnAfter1Year` and `initialTotalClaimable` are already set but `totalTitnClaimable`/`claimableTitnPerUser` are mid-update. An external protocol reading `titnBalance()` or `claimableTitnPerUser` during the callback sees stale values.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is a contract that receives TITN via `withdrawRemainingTitn`. 2) In the token's transfer hook, attacker reenters `claimTitn` or `withdrawRemainingTitn` to exploit the partially-updated state (e.g., `claimableTitnPerUser[msg.sender]` already zeroed but `totalTitnClaimable` not yet decremented, or vice versa). 3) Attacker extracts extra TITN or corrupts the proportional-share denominator.
hypotheses.impact: Double-claim or over-claim of TITN; incorrect `totalTitnClaimable` accounting; potential insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform all state updates (including `totalTitnClaimable -= claimableTitn`) before `titn.safeTransfer`, and ensure `titn` cannot be a hook-enabled token or use a pull-pattern.

hypotheses.title: quoteTitn uses block.timestamp, enabling same-block manipulation of titnOut
hypotheses.description: `quoteTitn` computes `titnOut` based on `block.timestamp - launchTime`. A user can time their `tgt.transferAndCall` to land in the same block as a favorable timestamp boundary (e.g., just before 90 days or just before 360 days) to maximize `titnOut`. Since `onTokenTransfer` credits `claimableTitnPerUser` based on this quote, a miner/validator or a user with mempool visibility can sandwich the boundary.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes pending `transferAndCall` transactions near a boundary (90 days or 360 days). 2) Attacker submits their own `transferAndCall` with higher gas to land in the same block just before the boundary, receiving the higher pre-boundary rate. 3) Attacker's `claimableTitnPerUser` is credited at the favorable rate, diluting the pool for others.
hypotheses.impact: Unfair distribution of TITN; users near boundaries receive more than intended; total `totalTitnClaimable` inflated relative to TITN reserves.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a block-number-based schedule or a fixed snapshot of `launchTime` with discrete epochs, and/or cap per-user claims per epoch.

hypotheses.title: Titn transfer lock can permanently freeze bridged holders' funds
hypotheses.description: When `isBridgedTokensTransferLocked` is true, any address in `isBridgedTokenHolder` (set automatically in `_credit` for every bridged recipient) cannot transfer tokens except to `owner()` or `transferAllowedContract`. On Arbitrum (chainid 42161), the restriction applies to ALL senders regardless of `isBridgedTokenHolder`. If the owner never unlocks or never sets `transferAllowedContract`, bridged users' tokens are permanently non-transferable — no user-side recovery path exists.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker bridges TITN to Arbitrum via LayerZero, becoming `isBridgedTokenHolder`. 2) Lock remains on (default true). 3) Attacker cannot transfer, sell, or move tokens; only owner-controlled paths exist. (Note: this is a design lock, but the untrusted actor's funds are trapped absent owner action.)
hypotheses.impact: Bridged users' TITN is frozen on Arbitrum; no permissionless exit.
hypotheses.recommendation: Provide a permissionless unlock after a deadline, or restrict the Arbitrum-wide restriction to bridged holders only and allow transfers to a user-chosen address after a timelock.

hypotheses.title: onTokenTransfer accepts TGT from any caller without signature or nonce binding
hypotheses.description: `onTokenTransfer` credits `claimableTitnPerUser[from]` based solely on `msg.sender == address(tgt)` and the `from` argument passed by the TGT token contract. There is no nonce, deadline, or per-transaction uniqueness check. If the TGT token is an ERC677-style token that allows a user to specify arbitrary `from` in `transferAndCall` (or if the token contract is upgradeable/malicious), an attacker can repeatedly invoke `transferAndCall` with the same `from` to accrue claimable TITN without actually transferring new TGT, or replay a previously observed transfer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a legitimate `transferAndCall` from victim to MergeTgt. 2) If TGT's `transferAndCall` does not enforce `from == msg.sender` or allows arbitrary `from`, attacker calls `tgt.transferAndCall(MergeTgt, amount, data)` with `from = victim`. 3) `onTokenTransfer` credits `claimableTitnPerUser[victim]` again, and the attacker can later claim on behalf of the victim or manipulate accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Duplicate crediting of claimable TITN, inflating `totalTitnClaimable` and enabling over-withdrawal of TITN from the merge contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `from == msg.sender` in `onTokenTransfer`, or verify the TGT token's `transferAndCall` semantics enforce caller identity; add a per-transfer nonce if the token supports it.
